about: Information shown on each sample's board (click a sample tube on the map). Keyed by sample number. "image": a path under public/ (e.g. "data/jezero/boards/roubion.jpg") or a URL; "imageCaption": credit or caption under it; "text": the description (blank lines start new paragraphs). Leave a field empty to hide it. "name" is only a reminder; the map uses the NASA sample list. Pairs from the same spot share one description: it is written in the first sample's entry, and the twin's text is left empty.

1.name: Roubion
1.text: The rover's first sampling try: the weathered rock crumbled, so the tube holds Martian air instead of rock. It is the first atmosphere sample, and a lesson to pick intact, less-pitted rock.

2.name: Montdenier
2.text: Two cores from one loose boulder on Artuby ridge, the first successful rock cores. They stand for the main crater-floor rock, less weathered here. Brace on bedrock: the boulder shifted while drilling.

4.name: Salette
4.text: Twin cores of coarse, olivine-rich rock in Séítah, the lowest and oldest rock on the crater floor. The crystals show to the naked eye, and it may link to a huge olivine-rich unit across the region.

6.name: Robine
6.text: Twin cores from layered bedrock in Séítah, near where it meets the crater-floor lavas above. Cores here can break apart, so a crew should plan a backup attempt.

8.name: Ha'ahóni
8.text: Two cores from the boulder Sid, only about 100 m from the landing site: the least altered crater-floor rock, key to dating the floor. It is very hard, so expect slow drilling and bit wear.

10.name: Swift Run
10.text: Twin sandstone cores from Hawksbill Gap, where the river delta met the lake. Grains washed in from a wide area, so one core samples many rock types, with cement that likely formed in water.

12.name: Hazeltop
12.text: Twin cores of fine lake mudstone rich in sulfate salts and clays, among the best rock for preserving signs of past life. A top-priority target in the search for ancient life.

14.name: Shuyak
14.text: Twin cores of olivine-rich lake mudstone at Cape Nukshak, where water partly turned the olivine into serpentine. Shuyak also holds traces of dating minerals such as zircon.

16.name: Kukaklek
16.text: Sulfate-rich lake-floor sandstone with calcium sulfate veins at Cape Nukshak. Another strong candidate for preserved signs of past life, with signals consistent with a mix of organic compounds.

17.name: Atmo Mountain
17.text: Loose soil from one wind-built megaripple: the sand and dust a crew walks on and carries back on suits and tools. Expect soft footing, with a coarse crust over finer sand.

19.name: Melyn
19.text: The first sample from the top of the delta: river sandstone that records the river which fed the lake. It sits about 120 m higher than the landing site.

20.name: Otis Peak
20.text: River gravel cemented into rock, holding pebbles from many source rocks. It carries the first iron phosphate found in Jezero.

21.name: Pilot Mountain
21.text: Poorly sorted river sandstone with carbonate cement, sampling the blocky river deposits on top of the fan. An earlier try on a boulder failed, so boulders make poor drilling targets.

22.name: Pelican Point
22.text: The first Margin sample, from the carbonate-rich strip by the crater rim that may mark an old lake shore. The outcrop is dusty, light-toned, fractured sandstone altered by water.

23.name: Lefroy Bay
23.text: Chosen because orbiters saw a strong carbonate signal here. Carbonates form in water and can hold climate records.

24.name: Comet Geyser
24.text: The most altered Margin sample, rich in carbonate and silica: a strong record of water reacting with rock.

25.name: Sapphire Canyon
25.text: Clay-rich rock cut by white veins and marked with pale "leopard spots" that may have formed through reactions microbes can also drive. With organic carbon detected, it is the collection's leading potential biosignature.
